title: Commentary Request
text: Backstage, I say.

“Great work today, everyone! You all put on a fantastic show again. Really… there was a time when we barely had enough acts to fill the program and I was at a loss, but thanks to everyone gathering together like this, our circus has grown to what it is now. Thanks again, truly!”
Everyone was brimming with motivation after receiving Father’s words of appreciation.
“Now then, food’s already prepared, so eat up and get ready for the next round. After that, you’re all free to do as you like!”

And so the circus’s time passed by like that, I say. When Father approached Itsuki, who stood looking bored in the corner backstage, Itsuki climbed straight up Father’s back as though it were his designated spot, settling onto his shoulders as a perch.
“So, how was it? What did you think, watching a bit of the stage from out there?”
“Seemed lively enough. The ending felt like it was trying to say that, race aside, everyone shares the same joy.”
“Yeah. That part carries a strong message from me, I think. The Filolials’ singing and dancing is so wonderful that I wanted it to look like everyone was having fun together because of it.”
“I can’t even go out there, though.”
Ren, being carried by Luna-chan, shot back at Father with half-lidded eyes as if lodging a complaint. Since he’d been treated as a tasty snack, he couldn’t exactly perform, I say.
“That grand finale’s the best, huh! Hey, Sword Bro, you should get in on the second-string circus too!”

Incidentally, Keel was permitted to appear in pig form, so she was mixed in with the group. The “second-string circus” was what Keel and the others called the circus over in Zeltoble. Father kept warning them about it, but the name kept slipping out anyway.
“No thanks. It’s already embarrassing enough being put on display, I’m not doing more of it.”
“Ehh, but everyone looks like they’re having fun trying to stand out even a little, don’t they?”
“Well, if everyone’s having fun and wants to stand out a bit, that makes me happy.”
Right? Father said, turning to look around at everyone, and they all got a little bashful.
“Gotta make the most of the fun times. If everyone’s having fun, the customers end up enjoying it too, apparently… it’s not like the backstage work is everything, after all.”

That’s right—we ran a circus while making our living through slave trading. And so, once the customers had headed home for the night, Father would go off to handle the slave trading. The bright, flashy hours out front came to an end, and the dark hours behind the curtain began. But first, dinner.

Before the circus started, Father and Panda’s foster father would team up to run a flashy food-stall show, and after the circus ended, that same cooking was served as a special meal to thank everyone who’d worked on the show. The crisp, rhythmic sound of chopping rang out—tack tack tack tack—as Father sent the ingredients he’d sliced flying through the air to Panda’s foster father, who deftly bounced them back with expert timing, tossing them into a pot or into a wok, stir-frying briskly with a sizzling clatter. Steamers were set up as well, and the simmering pots piled higher and higher with food.
“Count on you, aye?”
“Yeah, yeah.”

Father sliced through the ingredients at lightning speed, fully leveraging his stats. A cabbage-like vegetable sent flying was reduced to fine mince in an instant. Ren and Éclair stared at the sight, transfixed.
“Did you manage to catch that technique?”
“No… I couldn’t tell the angle he’s cutting at. Cut at the wrong angle and the vegetable would go flying apart.”
“It can’t just be about sharpness…”

Ren and Éclair stood there, groaning, staring intently at the cutting spectacle unfolding between Father and Panda’s foster father. Ren, hadn’t you gotten to the point where you could transform your weapon into the kitchen knife you’d been handed? In other loops you’d managed to pull off similar skills. Though it was ultimately just imitating Father, I say.
“Naofumi-san. Don’t you ever offer up some fancy commentary about the food?”
Itsuki asked between munching bites of the served dish, savoring it.
“Commentary? What do you mean?”
“You know, that sort of thing. Like ‘this dish is third-rate’ or ‘the ingredients are inferior’ or ‘this is barely edible’ or ‘this particular ingredient is the finest there is.’”
“That the rules of the dark culinary world, aye?”
Panda’s foster father asked back in turn, between bouts of cooking.
“Folk who like to draw clear lines with food tend to spin that kind of logic often enough, aye. Going on about how bad something is, or the reasons why it tastes so good.”
“Doesn’t that kind of exchange make the food taste worse if you’re eating while listening to it?”
“Aye, it does. It’s a bothersome sort of talk, the kind only a smooth-tongued sort who can turn black into white now and then bothers with.”
“Well… if there’s an actual problem, pointing it out that way isn’t necessarily a bad approach, I think.”
“Not saying you shouldn’t call out a real problem, aye. But is that the sort of thing you’re after here, getting all particular about fine dining?”

“Personally, I just think it’s enough if everyone’s satisfied and enjoys eating. I don’t think cutting corners is necessarily bad, but it’d be a problem if someone started bragging that their food’s better because of it.”
“Nothing to boast about, aye.”
So said Father and Panda’s foster father, but most everyone present apparently thought: look who’s talking.
“…Guess I asked that the wrong way. Let me put it differently then—if you could explain today’s dish in detail, I feel like it’d taste even better. So, please, enlighten me.”
“Huh?”
Father said, frying up cabbage minced cutlets to a perfect golden crisp at just the right moment and serving them up.

“It’s just… regular cabbage minced cutlets? The ingredients are a mix of ground meat from whatever monsters everyone hunted, minced together with cabbage-like vegetables and other veggies, kneaded, breaded, and fried. That about sums it up?”
“Made some meatballs alongside it too, aye!”
“Made hamburger steaks too, while we were at it. Cutting corners, cutting corners.”

It was ground monster meat, sure, but I understood something here. The blend ratio was completely different for every single dish, and Father and Panda’s foster father did it all unconsciously, I say. Surely no one but me would notice this, right? Panda, at least, was probably picking up on it—there were telltale movements suggesting an awareness of it. Anyway, calling it “cutting corners,” Father and the others were churning out huge quantities of similar dishes made from ground meat. It was a method specialized for versatility and mass production. And it was the kind of cooking method that any version of Father, across any world, just naturally did as a matter of course.
“Yay! Foooood!”
“Foooood! More, more!”
“Quite a fine flavor, this.”
Filo-tan, Kou, Yuki-chan, and so on—the Filolial-samas were all digging in too.
“…I want to hear something that makes it sound even more delicious, though.”

“Hmm… ah, how about this: ‘Wild brown usapil meat, aged to perfection in optimal conditions, luxuriously ground and combined with the meat of the frog salamander—a monster known for its mild yet vitality-rich flesh, similarly cultivated—then generously seasoned with the finest salt harvested from the seas near Lerno Village, along with vegetables and spices grown to magnificent perfection in the very earth of Melromarc, truly a single drop of the land itself, all fried into one exquisite dish!’ Something like that?”
“Isn’t that a pretty hollow-sounding way to put it?”
“Well, I mean… at the end of the day, it’s still just a ground-meat cabbage cutlet, isn’t it?”

“If you want it to sound even more delicious, aye, you’d add that the usapil’s thigh moves nimbly, used for kicking and fleeing, so it’s taut with muscle and thus packed full of flavor, aye. The part worked to its limits just to survive… you’d say something like how that strength spreads through the mouth as overflowing juices.”
“That sounds exactly like something someone who actually talks about usapil ingredients somewhere would say.”
“Heard that kind of talk before, aye. Or else how the oil’s made, that sort of thing.”

Ah, this one I knew, I say. Back on the road to Faubrey, Itsuki had asked about it once, when Father was frying things up over the campfire as though it were the most natural thing in the world. That time was…
“Naofumi-san. Isn’t it amazing that you can make fried food out in the middle of camping?”
“It’s not that hard when Motoyasu-kun handles the fire control for me, you know?”
“I get that part, but where did the oil even come from? Was it in the luggage somewhere?”
“Huh? It’s lard I made from the fat of the monsters everyone hunted, you know?”
“Lard, huh…”
“Ah, well, technically it’s not really lard—not pig fat. It’s a bit different from beef tallow too, so… monster fat, I guess you’d call it?”
